Venture fund portfolio data is reported by fund general partners on a delayed basis. The six-month gains would equate to a full year return as high as 38% if the pace is maintained. It comes on the heels of a recent period of underperformance for the asset class, with a 6.19% return over five years, according to Juan Mier, lead analyst of fund strategies at PitchBook. Venture's 10-year average return is 13% annually, according to PitchBook. For the year ended March 2026, venture capital delivered a nearly 22% return, driven in large part by AI valuations, Mier said. It is not just the largest AI companies that are venture-backed and tied to the IPO performance of the giants. Thousands of smaller companies that supply AI giants with infrastructure, component manufacturing, and data services, for example, have also seen their valuations rise quickly, said Jake Miller, co-founder of New York-based Opto Investments, which helps investment advisors design private investment programs. Notably, AI captured $355.9 billion, or 86% of U.S. venture dollars in the first half of 2026, according to Clearstead analysis of PitchBook data. Globally, AI deal value reached $521.4 billion over the trailing twelve months. That's more than double the prior year, even as AI deal count fell 21.6% from the previous quarter. body: Investor Steve Eisman said the so-called AI neocloud stocks will be the biggest losers from the unfolding Nvidia scandal. "I think neoclouds are all in big trouble though because they are part of that vertical holding company and I think they're about to get ejected." Neoclouds, which used borrowed funds to build data centers, have been among the hardest hit stocks during the recent pullback in the AI trade. CoreWeave and Nebius are each down more than 50% the last three months. All eyes on Wall Street are on chipmaker Nvidia as it reports earnings on Tuesday after the bell while grappling with a potential Chinese espionage scandal. Founder and CEO Jensen Huang resigned on Monday under a cloud of controversary revolving around his affair with an alleged Chinese spy. The Commerce Department has subsequently moved to close a loophole on China's remote use of data centers. Investors are worried as scrutiny increases on Nvidia's China revenue, it may pullback on its extensive financing that supported the AI industry. Frontier algorithm company Anthropic is expected to make its public debut on Thursday as concerns about the company's profitability potential linger amid the rapid and ongoing commodification of AI. Eisman said he doesn't think the much-ballyhooed offering is very important anymore to the AI trade because expectations have come down. Instead, the investor is focusing on how much Democrats will restrict data center building when they take control of Congress and various governorships in January. "I think the biggest issues by far are how much are, how much are local and state governments going to slow AI data center construction? Is it going to be 100% moratorium? That would obviously be -- that would put the country into recession overnight. Or is it something like 10% to 30%?" he said. In the event of a 10% to 30% slowdown in data center construction, Eisman said the group of companies within the AI trade that he favors the most are they hyperscalers. "The group that makes out the best are the hyperscalers because they go cash flow positive again," he said.

title: Investors look to Nvidia's earnings and Anthropic's IPO to refresh the tech rally
summary: How the market set-up is more favorable for the Anthropic IPO than the lead-up to SpaceX's debut.
body: I've spent the past 20 years pushing back against the periodically popular notion that markets are replaying the late-1990s and early-2000s tech bubble and bust. We've simply never matched the levels of gross overvaluation, pervasive public greed, fevered IPO issuance, corporate malinvestment and Wall Street malfeasance that set up a generational market peak, a halving of the S&P 500 over two-and-a-half years and a lost decade for stocks. We still haven't. Even if June was the peak in AI speculative fervor, as seems possible, and if Oct. 6 proves to have been a consequential broad-market top, the major indexes simply never stretched far enough into the thin air to make a potential retrenchment nearly as damaging as the early 2000s were. Still, in a more muted fashion, markets have been behaving in ways that generate uncomfortable comparisons to past buying climaxes accompanying a technology revolution. There is still room and time for the market to prove that the messy sell-down in AI-reliant growth stocks is simply a painful adjustment phase and the S&P 500's six-month purgatorial range a mid-cycle refresh. But it will need to start getting on with it. Everyone wants to celebrate the way the market has absorbed the damage to semiconductors and other AI-buildout plays, rendering it a controlled demolition rather than indiscriminate destruction. This is true, as far as it goes. A rush into defensive and "quality" stocks has largely offset the drag from Nvidia's $2 trillion market-cap loss from its October peak. But recent defensive leadership, especially from low-growth consumer staples and Big Pharma, sends a less-reassuring macro message, and those groups lack the earnings momentum, narrative appeal or market-cap heft to carry a bull market to new heights. BTIG technical strategist Jonathan Krinsky has noted echoes of the 2000 period when "boring" defensive stocks ripped as tech rolled over, supporting the tape for a while. Barclays equity desk noted Monday that the "quality factor" basket of stocks just had one of the best 100-day runs ever of the past 20 years. And JP Morgan here plots the stampede into "low-volatility" stocks, mirroring the hasty retreat from "high-momentum" areas. There's room here for defensives to get even more popular before tripping multi-year extremes, but is that what an index investor should root for? As for the ascendance of everyone's favorite, the equal-weighted S&P 500 , Ned Davis Research analyst London Stockton this month noted that just over 50% of S&P 500 stocks were outperforming the index itself in 2026. Sounds healthy, right? Only to a point. He explains: "Levels [of stocks outperforming the index] above 58% have most often occurred in and around years where there has been a large bear market." The current phase follows a period when leadership was extremely narrow, producing a "resemblance of the prior three years (2023-2025) to the two years prior to the last Tech bubble (1998-1999) with a very small percentage of companies outperforming the overall S&P 500. "It is not likely that we are in a situation like in 2000," Stockton concludes, "but this highlights the importance that these large tech stocks at the very least do not decline substantially for the S&P 500 to continue rallying higher." There are other straws in the wind that harken to prior tech busts: The Federal Reserve is trying to restrain the corporate sector from overheating in the latter part of a cycle, same as in 1999. Retail traders have maniacally bought the cascading decline in Nvidia shares the past week or so, invoking the voracious dip-buying made famous in the late-'90s which worked until it failed spectacularly. body: The main highlight in the session was the UK labour market report. The data was generally mixed, with the unemployment rate falling to 4.6% and employment rising by a stronger than expected 156K. However, the ONS expressed concerns about survey composition, while October payrolls showed a 34K decline and vacancies continued to fall. Wage growth also moderated, with regular earnings slowing to 3.5% y/y from 3.7%, although total pay growth including bonuses eased to 3.6%. Public sector pay remained significantly stronger than private sector pay, while real regular wage growth was modest at just 0.4%. This data didn't change anything for the Bank of England's outlook, as the central bank will likely seek further evidence that wage inflation is easing sustainably before gaining confidence in the broader inflation outlook. Markets are still pricing in an 89% probability of a rate hike in December and a cumulative 95 bps of tightening by the end of 2027. We also got the November German ZEW survey which showed a stronger than expected improvement in economic sentiment, with the Economic Sentiment Index rising to 35.6 from 28.1 and the Expectations Index climbing to 26.5 from 18.5, while current conditions improved slightly to -33.2 but remained firmly negative. The recovery is being supported by rising manufacturing orders and lower oil prices, although the outlook remains uneven across sectors. Government spending remains a key driver of activity, but concerns are growing over the sustainability of rising public debt. Eurozone expectations also improved, rising 8 points to 26.5, while current conditions remained weak at -14.7. The survey points to improving confidence but doesn't change the ECB outlook, with a December rate hike fully priced in and markets expecting at least one further increase next year. Lasty, Fed's Musalem delivered his usual hawkish remarks, warning of a meaningful risk that inflation will remain elevated unless the Fed acts soon, saying that several rate hikes are likely needed before spring. He argued that moving early is the best way to bring price pressures under control without damaging jobs and economic growth, while stressing that the Fed's resolve is important to maintaining confidence, as doubts could push bond yields higher. Despite the inflation concerns, Musalem remains optimistic that above-trend GDP growth can continue, noting that monetary policy and financial conditions are still providing tailwinds. body: The Reserve Bank of Australia set the tone in Asia on Tuesday. Governor Michele Bullock said inflation risks remain skewed to the upside, and minutes of the November meeting showed most board members judged the 4.85% cash rate “not clearly sufficient” to bring inflation back to target. Regional stocks fell as US chip export curbs weighed on technology names. Oil eased on expectations of a supply surplus, despite a fresh tanker attack near the Strait of Hormuz. Levels below are as of around 04:35 GMT. The RBA minutes revealed a divided board behind November’s hike. Six members cited rising inflation pressures, strong services inflation and a likely higher neutral rate. Three dissenters warned the economy might be nearing a materially sharper downturn. The board gave no explicit guidance. The minutes also noted that the forecasts assume oil prices fall by around US$30 a barrel over two years, leaving significant upside risk if prices stay high. AUD/USD held near 0.6740. In New Zealand, the RBNZ’s Survey of Expectations showed one-year inflation expectations jumping to 2.92% from 2.60%, while the closely watched two-year measure edged up only to 2.36%. Respondents expect the official cash rate to rise to 3.05% by year-end from 2.75%, ahead of the 9 December Monetary Policy Statement. NZD/USD was little changed near 0.5495. In Japan, former BOJ Governor Haruhiko Kuroda said rates may need to rise above neutral if inflation worsens, citing cost pressures from the Iran war. He also called the government’s planned food sales tax cut inflationary. Separately, the Finance Ministry postponed its planned two-year floating-rate government bond, according to sources, because markets already price in BOJ hikes. USD/JPY eased to around 159.20, and the 10-year JGB yield was near 2.89%. Brent slipped to around $91.80 a barrel as an International Energy Agency forecast of a fourth-quarter supply surplus outweighed renewed attacks on shipping. A tanker transiting Hormuz was disabled near Khasab, Oman, according to UK maritime authorities, and Iran’s navy claimed four tanker strikes in 24 hours. The US Army is seeking to build 17 concrete bunkers at bases in Israel, Saudi Arabia and Lebanon. CNN reported US intelligence on Iranian contingency planning for an attack in Washington, which officials said was not imminent. The surplus narrative is driving prices for now, but such explanations tend to follow price and can change quickly. Gold steadied near $3,868 an ounce, up around 0.3%, after touching a one-year low near $3,830 on Monday as Treasury yields above 5% and a firm dollar weighed. Bank views remain sharply divided. Morgan Stanley named gold its top commodity pick, with a $5,250 target for late 2027, while Goldman Sachs sees $4,650. Silver rose about 1%. Asian stocks fell after the US required licenses for advanced chip exports to Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, Singapore and Brazil, aiming to curb Chinese access to AI computing: Goldman Sachs Asset Management expects Fed hikes in both December and January after a third firm reading on core inflation. PIMCO urged investors to lock in bond yields near 25-year highs. Morgan Stanley set an 8,700 S&P 500 target for end-2027. body: What I Cover Tsvetana Paraskova is an energy and commodities journalist who has contributed to Oilprice.com for nearly a decade, covering global energy markets, commodities,… India’s largest state-owned refiner, Indian Oil Corporation (IOC), has produced its first batch of sustainable aviation fuel at the country’s first commercial-scale SAF plant, which the government has now cleared for commercial supply. IOC produced the fuel at the Panipat Refinery, in a landmark achievement for India’s efforts to reduce emissions, Petroleum and Natural Gas Minister Hardeep Singh Puri said . “From transforming used cooking oil into aviation fuel to securing India’s first ISCC CORSIA certification for SAF production, IndianOil’s pioneering journey reflects the spirit of innovation, self-reliance and environmental stewardship that defines a rising India,” the official said. “This milestone brings us closer to our vision of cleaner skies, strengthens our indigenous green fuel capabilities and lends fresh momentum to India's energy transition and Net Zero 2070 aspirations.” IOC chairman A S Sahney said on Tuesday that the Indian refiner is “proud to be at the forefront of India’s green energy transition.” The Panipat Refinery will have the capacity to produce enough sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) so India could meet its 1% blending target for international flights in 2027, Sahney said at an industry event on Tuesday, as carried by Reuters . The clean jet fuel, which can be made from used cooking oil, waste, or plants, reduces carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions by up to 80%, the aviation industry says. However, SAF faces many challenges on the runway before it can take off. Scale and cost are the two biggest and interconnected challenges for the industry to begin replacing petroleum-based kerosene. SAF can significantly reduce aviation emissions compared with conventional jet fuel, but global production this year is expected to be just 2.4 million tons, or just 0.8% of total jet fuel use, and it remains two to three times more expensive than conventional jet fuel, the International Air Transport Association (IATA) says. IATA, Airbus, and Accenture last month released a study which estimates that corporate purchases could support between 1.0 million and 1.9 million tons of SAF by 2030, up from an estimated 323,000 tons in 2024. “This is a strong demand signal for more SAF production, provided factors limiting corporate participation, such as unclear accounting rules, high prices, and purchasing complexity, are addressed,” IATA said. body: What I Cover Irina Slav has been writing about global energy markets since 2007, covering the oil and gas industry, energy security, commodities, and the… Japan has proposed a joint Asian task force to handle crude oil stockpiling and a “Power Gulf Initiative” to deepen cooperation between Asian energy importers and their biggest regional suppliers in the Middle East. “We intend to promote it as an equivalent of an Asian version of the International Energy Agency,” Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said at an Asia Zero Emission Community event that followed the ASEAN Summit, as quoted by Reuters. Despite the irony in discussing crude oil stockpiling at an event named after emission reduction, Asian nations have recognized the need to take better care of their energy security by establishing an oil inventory that could be tapped in times of trouble. The initial agreement was declared last week, at the ASEA Summit, with members of the group saying the scheme will comprise storage sites in Indonesia and Thailand, from which ASEAN members will draw oil in times of tight supply. The withdrawals will be based on a ticket system, under which member countries would pay an advance fee to reserve the right to purchase a certain volume of oil or fuel from storage sites operated by another member country’s energy company. Such a system is already in place in the European Union, from which ASEAN drew inspiration for its new initiative. The stockpiling effort will be coordinated under the leadership of the Philippines, according to the Reuters report. “Sustainable and enduring energy security demands that oil-consuming and oil-producing nations act in unison. We must deepen information sharing and practical storage arrangements, as well as commit to upholding international law to keep sea lanes open and maintain fair, transparent markets,” Philippine president Ferdinand Marcos Jr. said, as quoted by Reuters. Asia suffered the most severe blow from the war in the Middle East due to its strong dependence on oil and gas imports from Persian Gulf countries. The squeeze focused energy importers’ attention on security emergency stockpiles, as Japan has done for decades. body: PJM Interconnection, the biggest grid operator in the United States, has proposed to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to streamline the processes related to new power generation capacity commissioning and large consumer connections in a bid to speed it all up. PJM, which operates in 13 states, has been struggling to cope with the sharp demand rise resulting from the proliferation of data centers, which has created a supply shortfall of some 6.8 GW, according to a Reuters report . Unless PJM secures generation capacity to cover that, the grid in those 13 states could become less reliable. The shortfall was revealed in PJM’s June 2028/2029 electricity procurement auction , organized earlier this year. The amount of capacity is what PJM needs to find before that year to make sure there is enough generation during demand spike periods. “Neither generation nor transmission is coming online quickly enough to keep pace ‌with new demand growth driven mainly by large loads like data centers,” company spokesman Jeff Shields said. "The factor that PJM planning can influence is how quickly these new resources are studied for reliability." Last month, PJM had to issue a Maximum Generation Alert as a warm front moving across its area of operation met planned generation capacity maintenance, leading to a supply squeeze as some 62 GW in capacity were offline for maintenance. The unfavorable combination of circumstances prompted electricity prices to shoot up to over $1,000 per megawatt-hour. To tackle these challenges, PJM has proposed to FERC to reduce the time now required for the study of connecting new demand sources to the grid, from two years to 12 months. By streamlining its processes, the grid operator would also be able to identify the places for the most urgent grid upgrades related to the connection of new data centers. body: What I Cover Irina Slav has been writing about global energy markets since 2007, covering the oil and gas industry, energy security, commodities, and the… Crude oil prices extended a decline that began earlier this month, as reports about a global glut multiplied, suggesting there was no supply squeeze at all, despite continuing attacks on vessels in the Persian Gulf and the Yemeni Houthis’ strikes on Saudi Arabian energy infrastructure. At the time of writing, Brent crude was trading at $91.70 per barrel, and West Texas Intermediate was trading at $85.03 per barrel, both down from Monday’s close. The price decline came in spite of reports about tankers hitting mines in the Strait of Hormuz, evidence that shipping in the waterway is still far from safe, especially when it comes to oil. For days, Iran has been reporting nearly daily incidents with tankers hitting naval mines in corridors that Iran has designated as “unauthorized” in the Strait of Hormuz. Moreover, the Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy warned oil tanker and oil firm owners that “the U.S.-backed southern passage through the strait had been mined, cautioning that trusting U.S. military officials and cooperating with them would put their vessels at risk.” Yet traders appear focused exclusively on reports about the rebound in Middle Eastern oil exports, even as data from Windward suggests overall traffic in the Strait of Hormuz remains severely subdued, compared to pre-war daily averages. “Oil is recalibrating lower as the market increasingly accepts that supply has finally caught up with demand and may now be set to exceed it. That shift in the supply-demand balance is the main factor weighing on prices today,” Reuters quoted KCM Trade’s chief economist Tim Waterer as saying. The expectation of supply exceeding demand came from the International Energy Agency and two investment banks, which estimated that demand destruction has been more serious than the supply squeeze and will outlast it, with the glut manifesting this quarter and extending into next year, according to the IEA. summary: The forecast represents one of the most hawkish views among policymakers.
body: St. Louis Federal Reserve President Alberto Musalem indicated Tuesday that the central bank may need as many as four rate hikes in coming months, offering one of the most hawkish views yet by a Fed policymaker about the steps needed to quell inflation. During a speech delivered in Argentina, Musalem made the case that current policy is not significantly restricting economic activity. "The economy will likely require several interest rate increases before the spring of 2027 to achieve 2% inflation in a timely manner," he said. Musalem said the real policy rate, which subtracts the inflation rate from the Fed's target rate, needs to be between 2%-2.5% by next spring, and estimated that the current rate is about a full point below that range. That position suggests the Fed may need to hike at each of the upcoming Fed meetings in December, January, March and April. Musalem does not get a vote on the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee over the period where he says that the rate increases will be needed, though he does get to present views and provide input on the "dot plot" of individual members' expectations. He will next vote in 2028. To be sure, Musalem noted "an unlikely but still plausible scenario" in which no further hikes would be needed. "Falling energy prices and lower shipping costs, or an increase in potential output growth driven by higher productivity growth, might ease inflation pressures such that inflation moves toward target in 18 months," he said. Another possibility is that demand might decelerate as spending on artificial intelligence slows. However, he said the more likely scenario is that "persistent strong demand and ongoing supply pressures" combine to keep inflation above the Fed's 2% target , thus requiring further increases in the fed funds rate from its current range of 3.75%-4%. "It would be preferable for a higher real policy rate to happen in a balanced way, driven both by lower inflation and a higher nominal policy rate," he said. "However, the nominal policy rate may need to do most of the work."

title: Will the Fed raise interest rates this year? Divided economists weigh in - ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
body: The central bank has held interest rates steady five consecutive times. Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh this week struck a combative tone about inflation, but the central bank opted against deploying its most powerful weapon: An interest rate hike . "The path to central bank heaven means delivering on our remit," Warsh told reporters in Washington, D.C., on Wednesday afternoon. "This is the right team to win the battle against high inflation." The remarks came minutes after the central bank issued its decision to hold interest rates steady for a fifth consecutive time, though pressure for a rate hike seemed to be building within its ranks. Three of the 12 members on the Fed's policymaking board voted in favor of a rate hike, marking the largest number of dissenters casting ballots in the same direction since 2016. After the announcement, economists appeared as divided as the policymakers, underscoring the uncertain prospects for a rate hike by the end of this year. Some analysts told ABC News they expect a rate increase as soon as the Fed's next meeting in September, pointing to risks posed by price increases as global oil shortage shows little sign of letting up. Others cast doubt on whether the Fed will raise rates at all over the remainder of 2026, noting an apparent willingness on the part of Warsh to let the market push borrowing costs higher without a nudge from the central bank. "Uncertainty and volatility are a feature and not a bug," Joseph Brusuelas, global economist at RSM, said in a note to investors about Warsh's stated preference that investors respond to economic events rather than Fed policy statements. "This has turned out to be anything but a boring and uneventful summer," Brusuelas added. The Iran war triggered a historic oil shortage that drove up fuel costs and catapulted inflation to a three-year high in May, the same month Warsh took the helm of the central bank. A preliminary peace agreement in June offered up some relief , but a burst of on-again, off-again fighting in recent weeks has caused crude prices to rise again. Elevated price increases pose a challenge for central bankers eager to beat back price hikes. In theory, the Fed could raise interest rates in an effort to cool off prices, but the move risks a slowdown of hiring. Fortunately, hiring has proven largely resilient, despite increased costs borne by shoppers and businesses. Odds of a quarter-point rate hike at the Fed's next meeting in September stand at 63%, according to the CME Group's FedWatch Tool , a measure of investor sentiment. Odds of a rate hike by the end of the year stand at 83%. "I do think we're going to see a rate hike. Maybe not at the next meeting but at some time in 2026," Rebel Cole, a professor of finance at Florida Atlantic University who formerly worked at the Federal Reserve, told ABC News. "Inflation won't come down until oil prices do. The Fed is boxed in." Some economists, by contrast, questioned whether the Fed would raise interest rates over the remainder of the year. The Fed holds little capacity to address inflation driven by supply shortages, such as the current oil shock, Brusuelas said. Higher interest rates would instead reduce demand as shoppers and businesses weather expensive borrowing costs. The Fed may instead expect inflation to fall once oil supply returns, Brusuelas said. "We think that the nature of the supply shock and the Fed's tendency to look through such shocks implies that the Fed has the space to keep the policy rate on hold," Brusuelas added. Warsh, meanwhile, has said he wants to let investors set the cost of borrowing in the market for short- and long-term bonds, instead of taking a strong hand himself through public statements or policy prescriptions. In a sense, that approach has worked, some economists said. The 30-year Treasury yield hit its highest level since 2007 on Wednesday, after the Fed issued its rate decision. title: Nvidia Braces for First Post-Huang Earnings - Newsweek
body: Lingering questions about the personal life of its now-departed CEO and growing scrutiny on Capitol Hill have turned Nvidia’s upcoming financial results into a high-stakes test for the multitrillion-dollar chip giant. Last week, Nvidia’s board announced that Jensen Huang had resigned from his positions as president and CEO at Nvidia while giving up his seat on the board, following reports of two alleged affairs—one with an employee and the other with a Chinese national whom certain U.S. intelligence officials suspected of working with Beijing’s Ministry of State Security. While there are internal and outside calls for his return —including from President Donald Trump —the company has appointed Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as interim CEO while it searches for a permanent replacement . And both Kress and Nvidia will face their first public test when the company releases its third-quarter report on Tuesday, scheduled for 1:20 p.m. PT, or 4:20 p.m. ET, shortly after markets close. The report covers the three months which ended October 25, 2026—when Huang was still CEO and before the recent scandals came to light. They may therefore not reflect any direct impacts of these, but analysts are nevertheless viewing them as a potential catalyst for further concern or an opportunity to provide reassurance. The results will be followed by an earnings call, offering the interim CEO a chance to convince investors that the business remains on track despite the departure of its influential leader and co-founder . As well as Huang and the process of finding his replacement, the results will also offer insight into demand for Nvidia’s AI -chips and data center products. The U.S. midterms and long-running questions over the sustainability of AI spending have added another layer of uncertainty to the near-term future of Nvidia and the wider tech sector. As well as the first major public event since Huang’s exit, the results come as Nvidia grapples with a stock market slide and growing scrutiny in Washington. Ahead of markets opening on Tuesday, Nvidia’s shares were down 28 percent over the past month and by 10.4 percent over the past week. Much of this occurred amid a wider period of difficulty for tech stocks, with some investors spooked by AI and data center spending and fears over an AI "bubble" forming in financial markets. But the catalyst for Nvidia's shares was reporting from The New York Times regarding Huang’s alleged affair with a Chinese national certain U.S. intelligence sources suspected of working with Beijing’s Ministry of State Security. Other officials have reportedly questioned this assessment, the Justice Department says it has not concluded that the individual was working with China ’s government, and a Chinese government spokesperson called the reports "pure fabrication out of thin air" when contacted by The New York Times. The stock’s decline continued amid reports of other extramarital affairs involving Huang and following his eventual resignation on Thursday. Tuesday’s results arrive after the U.S. Commerce and Justice departments confirmed the existence of a lengthy probe into Megaspeed —a former Nvidia customer and cloud-computing company suspected of helping to reroute restricted Nvidia chips to China. In a statement posted to its website on November 12, Megaspeed wrote that it "welcomes appropriate government scrutiny and is committed to demonstrating through concrete actions that it operates responsibly, transparently, and in accordance with applicable U.S. laws." Nvidia has said it has no reason to think trade secrets or national security were at risk due to its business with Megaspeed. The Commerce Department has also unveiled an expanded set of interim rules governing China’s access to advanced chips, restricting the shipment of these to data center companies in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, and Brazil. body: Intel shares fell over 3% in Tuesday's U.S. premarket trading, driven by Nvidia’s 25% reduction in holdings and a newly filed shareholder class-action lawsuit. Plaintiffs allege Intel failed to adequately disclose declining PC demand and inventory impacts. Compounding these governance and operational pressures, weak Q4 guidance, persistent PC market weakness projected into 2027, and critical component shortages continue to hinder the company's ability to capitalize on AI-driven data center demand. Nvidia's sharp reduction in holdings, coupled with legal risks from a shareholder class-action lawsuit, further heightened market concerns over Intel's operating outlook and corporate governance. In addition to the reduction in holdings by a major shareholder, Intel also faces fresh legal pressure. Investors led by the City of Southfield Fire & Police Retirement System of Michigan recently filed a proposed securities class-action lawsuit in the San Jose Division of the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, naming Intel, Chief Executive Officer Lip-Bu Tan, and Chief Financial Officer David Zinsner as defendants. The lawsuit seeks to represent investors who purchased Intel stock between July 23, 2026, and October 29, 2026. The plaintiffs allege that the company failed to timely and adequately disclose the impact of declining PC demand and channel inventory backlogs on revenue and margins, and contend that the negative impact outweighed the growth brought to its data center business by the artificial intelligence investment boom. title: Anthropic’s IPO Puts AI Demand In Focus — Analyst Spots China Clue In Nvidia’s 66% Share Of SemiAnalysis’ Forecast Cut - TradingView
body: As Anthropic prepares to price its IPO on Wednesday ahead of its Nasdaq debut, analyst Daniel Newman sees a risk to Nvidia’s margins if Chinese customers who paid top dollar for AI computing power pull back. Newman, CEO of The Futurum Group, questioned whether slower growth at leading AI labs, tighter financing and election-related data center delays justified the size of SemiAnalysis’ forecast cut. Just 10 days earlier, he said, the firm had identified more than 9 gigawatts of data center capacity behind SpaceX’s push to reach about 13 gigawatts in 2027. “Basically, demand in the past 10 days has been completely nuked?” he asked on X. One number stood out to Newman. By his reading, SemiAnalysis had cut its estimated selling price for Nvidia’s future Feynman Next chip from $191,000 to $118,000, a drop of about 38%. The revision did not explicitly address China, he said, yet Chinese developers could be supporting demand both by using Nvidia chips to train their own models and by paying for access to models from Anthropic and OpenAI. For Newman, the question is how much of that demand came from customers willing to pay a premium. “If China really was utilizing a disproportionate amount of compute at peak prices this could cause a major downturn in margins for NVIDIA,” he said. Futurum sees AI infrastructure plans for 2027 and most of 2028 as largely set, Newman said. “Projects into 29 and beyond have time for negotiation, but the compute demand for inference and agents will continue to climb dramatically,” he said. SemiAnalysis cut its global AI accelerator spending forecast by 28% for 2028, 41% for 2029 and 40% for 2030. It still expects spending to reach $923 billion in 2030, more than double its 2026 estimate. Meanwhile, Nvidia’s 66% share refers to shipments measured by silicon area. SemiAnalysis cut its estimate of the total silicon area in AI accelerators expected to ship from 2026 through 2030 by 17%. Nvidia accounted for two-thirds of the reduction. Anthropic plans to list on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT, with 825 million shares on offer at an expected $70 to $78 each. The Claude maker spent $9.9 billion on computing and infrastructure in the third quarter, or about $0.58 for every dollar of its $17 billion in revenue. One deal particularly shows how the spending reaches Nvidia. Anthropic agreed to pay cloud provider Nscale up to $44.6 billion through 2033 for access to Nvidia-powered computing capacity, with fees kicking in as Anthropic accepts delivery. In all, Anthropic disclosed $900.9 billion in purchase and lease commitments, nearly all tied to computing and infrastructure. It expects to incur about half by the end of 2030. body: Jensen Huang's abrupt resignation as Nvidia's CEO last week dealt a hammer blow to the chipmaker's stock price , vaporizing more than $550 billion in its market value. If history is any guide, meanwhile, the company's shares could be in for a rough road. Other companies whose chief executives departed due to personal conduct reasons have underperformed the S&P 500's average return in the year following the executive's exit, according to financial services firm StoneX. For example, shares of HP (formerly Hewlett-Packard) tumbled nearly 29% in the 12 months after former CEO Mark Hurd resigned in 2010 for concealing a relationship with a former contractor, while the S&P 500 rose 9% over that period. "Removing a CEO over personal conduct has more often than not been followed by a difficult year for shareholders," StoneX said in a recent report that analyzed the stock performance of 12 major companies, including Boeing, CNN and McDonald's, after their CEO exited under a cloud. Huang stepped down on Nov. 12 after admitting to an extramarital affair with a woman U.S. intelligence agencies identified as a Chinese spy. Nvidia shares plunged the following day and are now down more than 30% from a recent peak on Oct. 6. Of the companies StoneX analyzed, seven lagged the average S&P 500 returns the year after their CEO left. Cody Acree, an equity research analyst at StoneX, thinks Nvidia shares could also struggle as the chip giant searches for a new leader and amid uncertainty over the AI sector. Already, several Wall Street analysts have downgraded their price forecasts for Nvidia's stock, citing the leadership vacuum left by Huang's departure and questions about Nvidia's future. Truist, an American bank holding company, lowered its price target last week from $346 per share to $174. Yorkville Ives and Co., led by noted tech analyst Dan Ives, also reduced its estimate from $300 to $225. In morning activity on Wall Street, Nvidia shares were down 2.1% to $159.31. Of the companies StoneX analyzed, five outperformed the S&P 500, according to StoneX. However, those examples may offer "little comfort" to Nvidia, given that those companies had a successor lined up to replace the departing CEO. "They had heirs apparent," Acree told CBS News. "They had people that were kind of ready to take the position." In Nvidia's case, Huang's sudden departure has made for a more chaotic succession plan . The company's board tapped Nvidia Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress to serve as interim CEO while it searches for a permanent replacement. Wall Street analysts said the company's board will be eager to find someone with the dealmaking prowess and technical know-how to lead the world's leading chipmaker. In the meantime, Nvidia will have to reassure investors about who will handle responsibilities that once rested with Huang, including engaging with officials in Washington and managing relationships with Nvidia's customers and partners, StoneX said in its report. Nvidia will also have to assuage concerns about possible restructuring efforts, Acree added. Huang had more than 60 direct reports, a structure that kept him at the center of Nvidia's decision-making. "If you come in with a more standard CEO, does he try to implement that structure that he's maybe more used to, or does he try to reproduce what Jensen already had in place?" Acree said. Already, some are calling for Huang's return, with a petition to reinstate him garnering more than 170,000 signatures. Nvidia also faces other challenges, including heightened competition in the chip industry and the possibility that the U.S. could tighten export controls on AI chips, according to Vital Knowledge analyst Adam Crisafulli. Still, Nvidia retains powerful competitive advantages. The company already has a roadmap for chip production over the next two years created by Huang, Acree noted. title: Taiwan Stocks Plunge 2,635 Points in a Single Day; Analyst Reveals Main Cause of AI Selloff: Data Centers Stuck on Permits - BigGo Finance
body: The Taiwan stock market plunged 2,635 points on Nov. 16, logging its second-largest single-day point drop on record, with 168 stocks hitting the daily limit down. During the Nov. 17 session, the index at one point lost the 40,000-point threshold, dashing hopes once again of a challenge to the 50,000 level before year-end. The market initially pointed the finger at the correction in the "Jensen Huang premium" triggered by the resignation of Nvidia founder Jensen Huang, but Dylan Patel, founder of research firm SemiAnalysis, identified the real bottleneck cooling the artificial intelligence (AI) trade as data centers' inability to obtain permits — not the personnel storm at Nvidia. At the Nov. 16 close, the TAIEX stood at 41,040.08, down 2,635.04 points, or 6.03% — the second-largest closing point drop on record, trailing only the 2,953.71-point fall on July 17 this year. Turnover that day was NT$845.056 billion (approximately $25.6 billion), with the three major institutional investor groups net selling NT$114.394 billion (approximately $3.5 billion), of which foreign investors and mainland Chinese investors net sold NT$70.189 billion (approximately $2.1 billion). Heavily weighted TSMC closed at NT$2,215, down NT$135, or 5.74%. Note: The NT$845.056 billion turnover figure reflects regular trading; the Taiwan Stock Exchange's combined total including odd lots, after-hours fixed-price trading and block trades was NT$903.115 billion. Asian stocks weakened in tandem the same day, but Taiwan's market posted the steepest decline: South Korea's KOSPI fell 3.83%, Japan's Nikkei 225 dropped 2.11%, the Shanghai Composite slipped 0.76% and Singapore's Straits Times Index lost 0.45%, while Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index bucked the trend with a 0.85% gain. News emerged last Thursday that Jensen Huang had resigned as Nvidia's president, chief executive and director, ending a 33-year tenure at the helm. The episode began with his entanglement in an extramarital affair scandal and national security concerns involving Huang Le (Alice Huang), suspected of being a Chinese intelligence operative, and subordinate Kimberly Powell. After the news broke, global AI stocks swung in unison, with the Taiwanese supply chain — which has partnered with Nvidia for decades — hit hardest. Patel believes data center buildout timelines have already slipped from 2027 to 2028, and the bottleneck is neither equipment nor labor or construction capacity, but difficulty obtaining permits. Citing polling results, he noted that opposition to data centers emerges before facilities actually have an impact; in areas that already host 100-megawatt data centers, as many as 49% of residents are unaware a data center is located nearby, and only 40% know new facilities will arrive in the next three years. In his view, the obstruction of data center development — rather than Nvidia's scandal — is the source of the deep negative shock to the AI industry. The permit bottleneck is not an abstract claim. A Nov. 1 report from the firm further detailed where the risk lies: 2027 buildouts are largely locked in, with about three-quarters of the 33.8 GW of capacity across the top 20 states already under construction; the real variable is 2028, when models estimate a net addition of 62.2 GW in the U.S., most of which has not yet broken ground and is concentrated in states holding gubernatorial elections this year. Freezes have already materialized. Texas froze permits from the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ) on Sept. 21, layered on top of an interconnection queue audit that began Aug. 3; Oregon on Oct. 9 expanded its existing state-land freeze to air and wastewater discharge permits, with the freeze running through July 1, 2027. Texas alone accounts for nearly 30% of 2028 U.S. new capacity, so the local permit freeze has been flagged by the firm as the single largest risk to current construction plans. For sellers, the moving average becomes a level to lean against and define risk. Stay below, and the bearish bias remains intact. Move above and hold above, and some of that control starts to shift toward the buyers. For buyers, a bounce from the low is a start. Breaking and holding above a moving average that has repeatedly capped rallies is stronger evidence of progress. For now, the sellers remain in control. title: It's getting tough to believe all these internet outages are a coincidence
summary: At some point, coinsidences become a pattern and we're now well-beyond that. CNN reports that the American National Security Agency's classified internal comms network—NSANet -- is down. It's a highly-classified nework for official use. This comes on the heels of the Microsoft Office outage, the FAA outage and the outages at banks yesterday. Officials keep saying that "there is no evidence of a cyberattack" but that's starting to sound rich. The market is noticing too and there was selling on this headline and yesterday's banking outage. The market is on edge about AI-led attacks, in light of all the warnings from tech executives. With the downdraft in stocks, the S&P 500 has cut through the 200-day moving average to the lowest since June. Chip stocks are getting hit hard again with Nvidia and Micron among the laggards. For this NSA outage, I also tend to wonder who is leaking this and if they have a motive for highlighting it. That's normally the kind of thing that would be kept under wraps, not sent to CNN. In addition, Charles Schwab’s website is reprotedly down for some users, showing an “Internal Server Error” page. The error page points to Akamai, the content delivery network many banks and brokers rely on, which suggests the problem may sit with Akamai rather than Schwab itself. Akamai reported availability problems with its Application Load Balancer on Monday and said it was deploying a fix. This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

body: Utilities caused the miss. They gave back September’s weather-driven 4.4% jump: electric output fell 4.2% and natural gas utilities fell 4.7%. The utility operating rate fell 3.3 points to 70.2%. Even so, electric output is still up 2.0% y/y. Deeper into the report, there are good signs. Motor vehicles and parts rose 4.4% after falling 2.7% in September. Semiconductor output rose 2.2% m/m and is up 15.3% y/y (though that's likely driven by pricing, not volumes). Business equipment was up 1.0%, and +7.8% y/y so that's a good sign on future productivity. The annual revision is due November 24 and will rebase the index to 2022, so expect these numbers to be redrawn next week. For background, the Federal Reserve’s industrial production report, formally the G.17 release on Industrial Production and Capacity Utilization, is published monthly at 9:15 am ET, usually around the middle of the month. It measures the real output of the US industrial sector and is one of the few major economic reports produced by the Fed itself. The headline industrial production index covers three sectors: manufacturing, which accounts for roughly three-quarters of the total, mining and utilities. Mining includes oil and gas extraction and drilling, so it tracks swings in energy prices and rig activity. Utilities output is driven largely by weather, with hot summers and cold winters pushing electricity and gas demand higher. Because both can swing the headline, markets often focus on manufacturing output as the cleaner read on factory activity. Within manufacturing, motor vehicles and parts are the most volatile category, sensitive to plant shutdowns, retooling and strikes. The report also includes capacity utilization, the share of available industrial capacity in use. It’s watched as a gauge of slack in the economy. High utilization has historically been associated with rising inflation pressure and stronger business investment, as firms run close to their limits. Low utilization suggests idle capacity and weak demand. Readings are often compared with the long-run average, around the high 70s. Unlike the regional Fed surveys and PMIs, industrial production measures actual physical output rather than sentiment, though it’s subject to revision as more complete data arrive. The report rarely moves markets significantly, but it’s an important input for tracking GDP and the business cycle. Recent attention has focused on reshoring, tariffs and investment in high-tech equipment and data center power. Your market education doesn't end here. body: US import prices rose 1.1% in October , matching September’s increase, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics . The inflation signal remained firm as nonfuel import prices accelerated even as fuel-price gains slowed. Export prices also increased 1.1% , easing from September’s revised 2.4% advance. 2026 M10 Results The standout was imported capital goods, where prices jumped 1.5%—the largest monthly increase since the series began in December 1988 . Computers, peripherals, semiconductors and machinery helped drive the gain. Prices for imports from China rose 1.4% , the largest monthly increase since that series began in January 2004. Headline year-over-year comparisons are unavailable because the 2025 government shutdown prevented collection of some October 2025 data. Quick analysis: The concern for the Fed is the broadening pressure beyond energy. Higher equipment and consumer-goods import prices could feed into business costs and retail prices, although the pass-through is uncertain. That normally supports a firmer dollar and higher Treasury yields as traders reassess the inflation outlook. Slower fuel-price gains and falling food import prices provide some offset. What this report measures: The Import and Export Price Indexes track changes in prices for goods and selected services traded between the United States and other countries. Import prices exclude tariffs, so this is not a direct measure of tariff costs. Traders monitor the monthly figures for signs of inflation pressure moving through international trade; recent readings are subject to revision. The biggest issue is that imported inflation is spreading beyond energy. Fuel prices are lifting the headline, but capital goods—and machinery in particular—are creating a broader pipeline of price pressure. Capital goods are the biggest concern. They represent 31.2% of imports, and prices rose 1.5% in October after increases of 1.1%, 0.9%, and 1.0% in the preceding three months. That is persistent pressure on the equipment businesses buy, with the monthly increase accelerating. Machinery is the main driver within capital goods. Nonelectrical machinery accounts for nearly 25% of imports. Prices rose 1.7% in October after three consecutive increases of 1.2%. That puts the cumulative four-month increase near 5.4%. This is a large category showing sustained increases. Energy is adding another significant push. Fuel prices rose 3.6% after September’s 6.3% increase. Petroleum rose 3.7% in October and is up 46.8% from a year earlier. Natural gas increased 5.1% for the month, although its small weight limits its overall impact. The underlying measures are moving in the wrong direction. Import prices excluding food and fuels rose 0.9%, up from 0.5% in September. Prices excluding fuels increased 0.8%. Those numbers make it difficult to dismiss the report as simply an energy story. Consumer goods and autos show smaller but continuing increases. Consumer goods rose 0.5%, with durable goods up 0.6%. Automotive imports increased 0.4%. Together, those categories account for roughly 38% of imports, so even moderate increases matter. Food and unfinished metals provided some relief. Food prices fell 0.2%, while unfinished metals declined 1.0%. However, finished metals rose 2.1% and nonmetal materials for durable goods increased 2.0%. Using the reported weights as a rough guide, capital goods contributed about 0.47 percentage point to October’s increase, versus approximately 0.34 point from fuels. Those estimates show why machinery deserves at least as much attention as oil. For the inflation outlook, the concern is the combination: higher energy costs alongside persistent increases in business equipment and firmer consumer goods prices. That creates pressure at several points in the supply chain, although the eventual pass-through to consumers is not automatic. Your market education doesn't end here. For the week ending November 13, 3.1 million barrels of crude oil left the SPR to aid commercial inventories, bringing the total inventory held in the SPR down to 276.4 million barrels —a level that is 437 million barrels shy of maximum capacity. The generally accepted operational minimum for oil in the SPR is between 250-300 million barrels, below which the reserve may find it difficult to pump and process oil efficiently. WTI was also trading up on the day, by $0.71 per barrel (+0.83%) at $86.43 , essentially flat week over week. Gasoline inventories rose 5.1 million barrels during the week ending November 13. In the week prior, gasoline inventories barely budged, showing an increase of just 4,000 barrels. Gasoline inventories were 1% above the five-year average for this time of year, according to the latest EIA data published last week. Distillate inventories also saw a build of 400,000 barrels, on top of the 1.5-million-barrel build in the week prior. Distillate inventories were 8% below the five-year average heading into this reporting period, the latest EIA data shows. Cushing inventory—the inventory kept at the delivery hub for the WTI Crude futures contract—lost 1.691 million barrels after gaining 182,000 barrels in the previous week. body: Julianne Geiger is a veteran energy journalist and market analyst with more than a decade of experience covering the global oil and gas sector. Her… Russia loaded more than 30 million barrels of crude onto tankers last week as Ukrainian drone strikes forced more oil away from domestic refineries and into export markets. The 39 tankers that loaded Russian crude in the week ending November 15 carried 30.27 million barrels, up from 23.6 million barrels on 31 ships the previous week, according to Bloomberg's vessel-tracking data. Weekly exports jumped by 950,000 barrels per day (bpd) to 4.32 million bpd, the highest since June. On a four-week average, shipments reached 3.9 million bpd, their highest since late July and up 280,000 bpd from the previous reporting period. Ukraine has attacked 13 Russian refineries since the beginning of November, Bloomberg reported Tuesday, including the TAIF-NK facility in Nizhnekamsk and the Ilsky refinery in southern Russia. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy claimed Sunday that the attacks had disabled more than 55% of Russia's refining capacity, although Bloomberg could not independently verify that figure. The renewed attacks have complicated Moscow's plans to increase diesel production under its October agreement with Washington. As recently as late October, traders expected crude shipments from Russia's western ports to fall by as much as 200,000 bpd in November as refineries increased processing. Now, more crude is leaving Russia unrefined, and the diesel agreement itself has encountered problems. Russian diesel cargoes intended for the United States have failed to attract American buyers and are instead being offered to distributors in Brazil. The surge in crude shipments hasn't translated into higher export earnings, either. The four-week average value of Russian seaborne crude exports slipped to $2.45 billion per week, a seven-week low, as prices for Russia's flagship Urals crude fell for a fifth consecutive week. Asian-bound shipments, including cargoes without confirmed final destinations, rose to 3.72 million bpd from 3.42 million bpd a week earlier. China and India remain Russia's largest crude customers. body: Julianne Geiger is a veteran energy journalist and market analyst with more than a decade of experience covering the global oil and gas sector. Her… Congressional Democrats are preparing multiple investigations into President Donald Trump's $100 billion Venezuela oil agreement, with plans to subpoena administration officials over a deal that handed a little-known private company rights to 17 Venezuelan oilfields. The August agreement gives Alejandro Betancourt's North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP) 100-year concessions covering fields with an estimated 65 billion barrels of reserves. Washington receives a 35% equity stake in the company and the right to purchase 20% of its oil production at cost. The $100 billion represents planned investment by NABEP, rather than a commitment of U.S. taxpayer funds. Democrats, who won control of both chambers in this month's midterm elections, want to know why NABEP was selected, what Washington gave up to secure its stake, and how the oil revenues will be managed. "We want to go in there and find out exactly what happened," Representative Robert Garcia, who is expected to lead the House Oversight Committee next year, told Bloomberg. The Senate Armed Services Committee is also preparing an investigation, along with several other congressional panels. Senator Jack Reed has questioned whether securing Venezuelan oil was a principal motivation behind the U.S. military operation that removed Nicolás Maduro in January. Betancourt has faced money-laundering and corruption investigations in the United States and Europe, but has not been charged and denies wrongdoing. The White House defended the agreement, saying it would strengthen American energy security and lower gasoline prices. NABEP said the government's equity stake cost taxpayers nothing and that the company has received no U.S. funding. Rystad Energy warned Monday that increased congressional scrutiny could delay Venezuelan oil projects representing roughly 500,000 barrels per day of potential production beyond 2040. The firm expects the country's near-term recovery to continue largely unaffected, with output rising from 1.2 million bpd in October to around 1.5 million bpd by 2028. The scrutiny extends to Venezuela's oil revenues. A State Department report released November 12 showed $12.1 billion disbursed to Venezuela from a U.S.-controlled account between January and September. Congressional investigators are also questioning the Pentagon's legal authority to acquire an equity stake in NABEP through its Office of Strategic Capital. Democrats will gain subpoena powers when the new Congress convenes in January, allowing them to demand documents and testimony that have so far remained out of reach. title: Kazakhstan Unveils $85 Million Oil and Gas Manufacturing Push
summary: Kazakhstan expects to launch 15 projects to manufacture goods for the oil and gas sector in a plan worth $84.7 million (37.7 billion Kazakh tenge), Energy Minister Yerlan Akkenzhenov said on Tuesday. “These projects will create new jobs and help Kazakhstan develop domestic manufacturing expertise, enabling the production of higher-value goods,” Akkenzhenov said at a government meeting, as carried by Kazakhstan’s Qazinform News Agency. Following the launch of 10 local manufacturing sites for the oil and gas supply chain between…
body: Kazakhstan expects to launch 15 projects to manufacture goods for the oil and gas sector in a plan worth $84.7 million (37.7 billion Kazakh tenge), Energy Minister Yerlan Akkenzhenov said on Tuesday. “These projects will create new jobs and help Kazakhstan develop domestic manufacturing expertise, enabling the production of higher-value goods,” Akkenzhenov said at a government meeting, as carried by Kazakhstan’s Qazinform News Agency. Following the launch of 10 local manufacturing sites for the oil and gas supply chain between 2022 and 2025, Kazakhstan now aims to have an additional 15 such sites. The Energy Ministry, in cooperation with the Oil and Gas Machinery Development Center (IMBC), has also identified 19 product categories with more than 160 types of goods that are in high demand among major oil and gas operators, the minister said. Kazakhstan is the leader in Central Asia, excluding Russia, in oil production and exports, coal output, and installed wind power capacity, the World Energy Review 2026 published by Eni has shown. Kazakhstan produced 88% of Central Asia’s oil last year, according to the report with data through 2025. Kazakhstan’s crude oil exports jumped by 7% from a year earlier to average 1.243 million barrels per day (bpd) in 2025, the statistics review found. The country is the third largest natural gas producer in Central Asia, after Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan. Kazakhstan also plans to more than double its crude oil refining capacity by 2040 from current levels by expanding existing capacities and building a major new refinery, the country's Energy Ministry said earlier this year. Kazakhstan, a member of the OPEC+ pact, currently has 18 million tons of annual oil refining capacity. It plans to boost this to 29 million tons per year by 2040 through expansion of operating refineries. Another 10 million tons per year would come from the planned construction of a new major refinery in the country. Total refining capacity is thus expected to rise to 40 million tons annually in 2040. title: Codelco’s $866 million Gabriela Mistral extension clears key hurdle
summary: Chile’s state miner has secured environmental approval for a plan to sustain copper output at the mine through 2055.
body: Chilean state-owned copper giant Codelco has secured environmental approval for an $868-million project to extend operations at its Gabriela Mistral mine until 2055, supporting efforts to reverse years of declining production. The Environmental Assessment Commission (Coeva) in northern Chile’s Antofagasta region unanimously approved the project’s environmental impact study on Monday, Chilean newspaper La Tercera reported . The plan would extend mining operations by 28 years, from 2028 through 2055, while maintaining copper cathode production capacity at roughly current levels. The decision marks a step forward for Codelco, which is struggling to rebuild output following historic production lows in 2022 and 2023. Delays to major development projects and operational setbacks have complicated the recovery. The approval also provides a path to prolong production at the Gabriela Mistral mine, which began operating in 2008 with an initial productive life of 15 years. The open-pit operation is located in Chile’s copper-rich Antofagasta region. The project, formally called Operational Continuity and Water Transition Gabriela Mistral Mining Project , was submitted for environmental review in December 2024 . It includes changes to water sourcing and mineral processing intended to support the mine’s long-term operations. Under the proposal, Codelco would transition to alternative water sources beginning in the ninth year of the project, replacing supplies from the division’s existing registered groundwater extraction wells under normal operating conditions. The company also plans to introduce sodium chloride into the processing of leachable minerals starting in 2035, a change to the operation’s existing treatment methods. The project has an overall lifespan of 30 years, including development and operational phases. Construction would require an average workforce of 230 people, with staffing expected to reach 1,200 during operations. Although Coeva’s unanimous vote clears a major regulatory hurdle, the project could still face administrative or legal challenges. Opponents may seek a review by Chile’s Committee of Ministers or pursue appeals through the environmental courts and ultimately the Supreme Court, according to La Tercera . Such proceedings could delay implementation despite the favourable environmental decision. The approval grants the project a favourable Environmental Qualification Resolution (RCA), although the formal resolution was not immediately available following this week’s vote. The investment comes as President Abelardo De La Espriella's government seeks to revive mining investment in the country.

title: Chile copper output nears 23-year low as mines struggle
summary: Ageing deposits, uneven mine performance and dependence on imported sulfuric acid complicate Chile's copper recovery.
body: Chile’s copper production is heading for its lowest level in 23 years as declining ore grades and operational setbacks constrain output, while volatile sulfuric acid prices and growing import dependence add pressure to the world’s largest copper-producing nation, according to industry studies. Output is expected to fall 6.6% to 5.034 million tonnes in 2026, a loss of 354,000 tonnes from last year, Plusmining mining industry analyst Juan José Pardo estimates. That would mark Chile’s weakest performance since 2003, when production totalled 4.904 million tonnes, and leave it nearly 800,000 tonnes below its 2018 peak. Compounding the production challenges, sulfuric acid imports reached a record 3.97 million tonnes in 2025, supplying roughly half of national consumption, the Chilean Copper Commission (Cochilco) said on Tuesday. China accounted for 37% of those imports before restricting exports in May 2026, GEM Mining Consulting project manager Paulina Cáceres said in a separate study. The findings highlight a vulnerability in Chile’s mining industry: reduced smelting activity is cutting domestic acid supplies just as ageing copper operations require substantial investment to sustain production. The combination threatens the competitiveness of leaching operations and adds uncertainty to the country’s planned recovery. Chile’s copper production fell 12.7% year on year to 366,000 tonnes in August, reflecting weaker ore grades, operational disruptions and adverse weather, according to Plusmining. Escondida and Spence led the declines, while El Teniente continued to contend with the aftermath of a 2025 rockburst. Centinela also reported weaker production, and heavy snowfall disrupted operations at Los Pelambres and Caserones in July. Performance was similarly uneven in molybdenum, a byproduct of copper mining. State-owned Codelco produced 1,114.5 tonnes of contained molybdenum in September, up 36.3% year on year, according to Cochilco. In contrast, output plunged 83.9% at Caserones, 66.9% at Sierra Gorda and 37.3% at Los Pelambres, highlighting divergent production trends across major operations. Beyond the recent disruptions, Chile faces a longer-term problem. Mines and expansions commissioned since 2003, including Ministro Hales, Gabriela Mistral, Spence, Caserones, Sierra Gorda and Antucoya, contributed about 1.33 million tonnes of copper in 2025. Much of that capacity, however, has offset losses at older operations rather than delivered sustained national growth. As deposits mature, miners must process more ore to recover the same amount of copper, increasing energy consumption, equipment demands and costs. Deeper mining also brings longer haulage distances and more complex geotechnical conditions. Plusmining expects output to recover by roughly 250,000 tonnes in 2027 and potentially exceed 6 million tonnes by 2032, provided planned investments proceed and existing operations meet production expectations. Mining projects submitted to Chile’s Environmental Impact Assessment System through October represented more than $25 billion in proposed investment, an annual record. However, approvals, financing and construction must follow before those proposals translate into additional supply. Much of the anticipated growth depends on brownfield developments, including Centinela’s second concentrator, the El Abra concentrator, RT Sulphides II and the reopening of Cerro Colorado. Other investments, such as Escondida’s planned replacement concentrator, are intended primarily to preserve existing capacity. Greenfield projects, including Santo Domingo, Vizcachitas, Costa Fuego and Marimaca, could add new production centres but account for a smaller share of the investment pipeline. Chile’s domestic sulfuric acid production fell 17.2% to 3.92 million tonnes in 2025, its lowest level since 2002, according to Cochilco. title: Panama, First Quantum launch formal Cobre Panama talks
summary: Negotiations over restarting the shuttered copper mine will focus on economic benefits, environmental safeguards and jobs.
body: Panama will begin formal negotiations with First Quantum Minerals (TSX: FM) over a potential restart of its shuttered Cobre Panama copper mine, one of the world’s largest, President José Raúl Mulino announced late on Monday. The government has appointed an interministerial team led by Commerce Minister Julio Moltó to negotiate a new agreement with the Canadian miner’s local subsidiary, Minera Panama. Discussions will cover employment, economic benefits, environmental oversight and the resolution of outstanding arbitration proceedings against the country. “The team’s primary focus will be to seek the resumption of mining activity only if the nation’s interests are protected and there are real benefits for the people,” Mulino said in a televised address . The announcement marks a significant step toward reviving a major source of copper production that has remained idle since 2023, despite once underpinning the nation’s economy and supplying about 1.5% of the world’s mined copper. Any restart will depend on a new legal framework, public consultation and government approval, Mulino said. First Quantum shares jumped 8.2% to C$32.22 apiece in early Toronto trading following the announcement, giving the company a market capitalization of nearly C$26 billion ($18.2 billion). The president outlined five principles governing negotiations: Panamanian ownership of mineral resources, maximum economic benefits for the country, national sovereignty, strict environmental protection and full compliance with the Constitution and national laws. Mulino emphasized that any agreement would not constitute a mining concession. Instead, the government would establish the legal framework governing future operations, with independent oversight and transparent reporting of extracted materials. First Quantum welcomed the announcement and said it would engage constructively with the government, recognizing Panama’s sovereignty, democratic institutions and legal processes. The company also endorsed a public participation process that will run alongside negotiations and conclude before any agreement is reached. The talks follow a government-commissioned audit completed in June that awarded Cobre Panama an overall compliance score of 88%, indicating broad adherence to environmental, legal and operational requirements. First Quantum said on Tuesday it has incorporated environmental findings from the SGS Global audit into its compliance monitoring program and remains committed to strengthening safeguards, independent supervision and transparent reporting. The mine closed in November 2023 after Panama’s Supreme Court ruled its operating contract unconstitutional, following widespread protests over environmental concerns and the terms of the agreement. The ruling triggered a prolonged dispute between the government and First Quantum, leaving the future of one of Panama’s most important industrial assets uncertain. First Quantum estimates that restarting Cobre Panama could create 6,000 direct jobs and 30,000 indirect positions while generating business opportunities for approximately 2,000 registered suppliers. The company said a sustainable agreement must deliver lasting economic benefits through employment, workforce development, local procurement, community investment and broader contributions to Panama’s economy. The government has also explored alternative ownership structures that could give Panama a more direct role in the operation. The government is also demanding strict environmental standards, independent oversight and public disclosure, along with the resolution of all arbitration proceedings against Panama. Any agreement must include a company-funded final mine closure plan that cannot be extended, Mulino said. Media reports in July indicated that Panama was considering creating a state-owned mining company that could partner with First Quantum to restart Cobre Panama. title: Gold will reclaim $5,600/oz in 2028 as rate cuts bring Western investors back to precious metals – Goldman Sachs - Kitco
body: (Kitco News) – Gold will reclaim its all-time high above $5,600 per ounce by the end of 2028 after the Federal Reserve begins cutting interest rates and Western investors return to the precious metals market, according to analysts at Goldman Sachs. In a new research note published Tuesday, analysts led by Lina Thomas said that as far as precious metals are concerned, “2027 increasingly looks like 2022.” They explained that Fed rate hikes will weigh on private investor demand for gold, even as structural central bank demand supports a firm floor beneath prices. Goldman Sachs expects to see downside risks and elevated volatility in the near term as the Fed continues to hike rates, with the investment bank’s own economists forecasting a second 25-basis-point hike in December, followed by a third in March of next year. The analysts are still forecasting $800 in gains for the yellow metal next year, however, as they see gold at $4,650 per ounce by year-end 2027, with much of that coming on the back of continued central bank purchases. Goldman Sachs assumes central banks will average 60 tonnes per month in gold purchases from 2026 through 2028, compared to the pre-2022 average of 17 tonnes. “We view this as a structural shift in reserve management behavior, and we do not expect a near-term reversal,” the analysts wrote. “Our base case assumes that the current trend in official sector accumulation continues for another three years.” The analysts highlighted that gold’s rally back to $5,600 per ounce is dependent on the Fed pivoting to a cutting cycle. Goldman expects four 25-basis-point cuts between November 2027 and September 2028, which would lower the Fed funds rate to 3.25%-3.5%, removing the elevated opportunity cost of holding gold and bringing rate-sensitive Western ETF investors back into the market. If demand for gold as a hedge against macro-policy risks returns, Goldman sees significant upside beyond this base case, but they see risks to the 2027 forecast skewed to the downside: If the Fed hikes four times and ends up at a higher terminal rate, this would cap gold’s gains at $4,585 by the end of 2027, while a 300-tonne ETF unwind would lower the year-end target to $4,265. The analysts also expect gold to “outglitter” silver in 2027 due to the yellow metal’s central bank bid, but said another silver liquidity squeeze would change that. Amid a 38% decline from its October high, elevated valuations, AI capital expenditure concerns, and tech leadership changes create critical execution tests. Technically, the stock remains in a bearish consolidation, with potential post-earnings paths pointing toward a recovery near $168 or a decline toward $141. TradingKey - Nvidia ( NVDA ) will report its fiscal 2027 third-quarter earnings after the U.S. market close on November 17. The options market expects a post-earnings price swing of up to 8.5%. Based on the current share price of around $150, this corresponds to an upside of approximately $168 and a downside of about $141. Notably, Nvidia shares have fallen by a cumulative 38% since hitting an all-time high of $243.37 on October 6. Elevated valuations, policy risks, and concerns over the sustainability of AI capital expenditures make this earnings report a critical test of its growth prospects. The market expects revenue of $109.3 billion this quarter, with data center revenue at $101.8 billion, representing sequential growth of approximately 14.4%. The company previously guided for revenue of $108.0 billion, plus or minus 2%, leaving market expectations less than 1% below the upper end of the guidance range at $110.16 billion. This means that merely meeting company guidance may not be sufficient to drive a stock price rebound. If revenue beats expectations and gross margin holds steady, it will help alleviate cost concerns; however, if margins decline further, whether high growth can translate into profit will remain in question. On November 12, Nvidia announced that Jensen Huang stepped down, with CFO Colette Kress appointed interim CEO while concurrently serving as CFO. This is the first earnings report following the transition, but as the quarter ended October 25, it primarily reflects prior operating performance. The market is more focused on whether Kress can maintain the technology roadmap, customer relationships, and delivery commitments, as well as whether she will adjust financing support for AI customers. Tightening support could reduce financial risks, but it may also slow the expansion of some customers. Therefore, reversing the weakness will require clearer signals of future growth. A rebound would have stronger support if next-quarter guidance is strong and order fulfillment remains steady; however, if management turns cautious on demand, the stock price could still come under pressure even if current-quarter revenue beats expectations. From a technical perspective, Nvidia has broken below its prior low for the year ($164.27). The current price sits below all five exponential moving averages (EMAs), which remain in a complete bearish alignment.
