body: The outlook for crude oil prices has shifted considerably since the onset of the U.S.-Iran war. While escalating geopolitical tensions initially triggered a sharp rally and heightened volatility, recovering oil exports, easing geopolitical risk premiums and growing expectations of a global supply surplus recently weighed on prices. As a result, oil prices have declined substantially from their October highs. Brent crude, which ended October at approximately $113.40 per barrel, is currently trading around $92.5, while WTI crude has fallen from nearly $104 to approximately $85.8 per barrel, reflecting declines of approximately 18.48% and 17.64%, respectively, and highlighting the significant correction in crude oil prices. This significant decline reflects a shift in market sentiment, as concerns over prolonged supply disruptions gradually give way to expectations of recovering oil supplies and a potential global supply glut. Goldman Sachs and the International Energy Agency (IEA) are both forecasting a potential global oil supply surplus. As reported by Bloomberg and cited by OilPrice.com, commodity analysts at Goldman Sachs expect global oil supply to outstrip demand by approximately 2 million barrels per day next year. Goldman Sachs analysts forecast Brent crude prices to average $88 per barrel in 2027, with prices projected to ease to approximately $78 per barrel toward year-end. However, the bank also cautioned that ongoing supply disruptions could pose a risk to this outlook. The widening gap between global oil supply and demand was also highlighted by Goldman Sachs, which pointed to weakening consumption in China and rising production in the Middle East. As quoted on the abovementioned article, the divergence in supply and demand is also highlighted by the bank. Goldman Sachs noted weaker demand for crude in China because of a decline in transport fuel demand. The bank expects a decline in transport fuel consumption to reduce China's overall oil demand by approximately 400,000 barrels per day in 2027. At the same time, it anticipates Middle Eastern oil production to increase from 2025 levels, further weighing on international crude prices. Goldman Sachs cited the growing use of ship-to-ship transfers and the addition of new pipelines as factors supporting higher regional output. According to a Reuters article, the IEA also expects the global oil market to return to a supply surplus as early as this quarter, as exports from the Middle East recover at a faster pace than global demand despite ongoing attacks on shipping. The agency projects oil supply to average 105 million barrels per day (bpd) in the current quarter, outstripping demand by 1.7 million bpd. This represents a reversal of its previous outlook, which had pointed to a supply shortfall during the quarter. Additionally, easing geopolitical risk premiums could put additional pressure on crude prices. As quoted in another Reuters article, oil tanker freight rates have fallen sharply since the start of November, reflecting softer chartering demand and a gradual unwinding of the geopolitical risk premium. According to Baltic Exchange data, as quoted in the abovementioned Reuters article, freight rates for very large crude carriers (VLCCs) transporting oil from the Gulf of Oman to China dropped to around 308 on the Worldscale index on Nov. 13. This represents a 64% decline from the record high of 841 recorded on Oct. 8. Per the Reuters article, shipping costs fell even more sharply along other major routes, particularly those connecting West Africa with Asian markets. Investors expecting oil prices to decline further amid weakening market fundamentals may find short-term bearish positioning increasingly attractive. Against this backdrop, inverse energy ETFs could offer a tactical way to capitalize on further weakness in crude oil prices. body: The latest U.S. petroleum balance is a mixed signal for West Texas Intermediate crude. The EIA report for the week ending November 6 showed commercial crude inventories rising 4.7 million barrels to 414.4 million. Gasoline stocks increased 1.8 million barrels to 210.8 million, and distillates added 4.1 million to 103.3 million. These product builds matter because they suggest that the refinery system was supplying the market faster than final demand for transport fuels during that week. A single weekly movement, of course, is noisy, but the combination does not support a convincing near-term storage story. At the same time, refinery activity was strong. Crude inputs at U.S. refineries averaged 17.047 million barrels per day, up 322,000 barrels per day from the prior week. That is supportive of crude consumption. Refiners were taking in more feedstock even as crude inventories increased. U.S. field production was estimated at 14.013 million barrels per day, while imports averaged 6.698 million barrels per day and crude exports 3.455 million barrels per day. The weekly figures are estimates and can be revised. They are best read together as a snapshot of the domestic balance rather than proof of a durable trend. A four-week average of crude exports is more informative than one weekâs flow, and the report puts it at 3.857 million barrels per day. The marketâs next test is whether higher refinery runs persist and whether product stocks begin drawing as colder weather and transport demand evolve. If runs remain high while gasoline and distillate inventories turn lower, the crude build could prove temporary. If product stocks continue to rise, refiners may have less incentive to sustain utilization, leaving more crude in storage. The next EIA weekly petroleum release is the first clear domestic check on the balance. EIAâs November outlook forecast record U.S. crude production of 14.3 million barrels per day next year, up from an estimated 13.9 million barrels per day this year, while commercial inventories remain below their five-year average into 2027. Growing supply, therefore, may be absorbed if refinery demand and exports remain firm. During the session here on Tuesday, we have seen a significant amount of strength, but it still looks like a market that is hanging around the 200-day EMA and consolidating more than anything else. This is not a market that is waiting for the next signal. Every new Brent Oil analysis as it publishes, today's technical signal and key levels, live price â on one page. Brent marketâs global backdrop is less one-sided. In its November 13 Oil Market Report , the International Energy Agency estimated that world oil supply rose 2.3 million barrels per day month over month in October to 105.4 million barrels per day, following an increase of 3 million barrels per day in September. Higher Gulf exports drove most of Octoberâs gain. The same report estimated that observed global inventories rose 52 million barrels in October, or about 1.7 million barrels per day, the first increase since June. The inventory headline needs qualification. The IEA said oil on water increased by 86 million barrels to its highest level since January, while on-land stocks remained at their lowest since 2016. OECD industry inventories fell 41 million barrels during October within a broader OECD stock decline of 47 million barrels. In other words, more crude and products were counted in the global system, but much of the gain was cargoes at sea rather than immediately available barrels. Longer voyages and elevated freight costs can delay the point at which those barrels ease local tightness. Demand expectations also point towards a looser balance. The IEA forecasts demand falling 2.7 million barrels per day in 2026 to 102.3 million barrels per day, then rebounding to 2 million barrels per day in 2027. It sees supply declining by 4.8 million barrels per day this year before recovering 6.6 million barrels per day next year.

Warsh Lays Out Three AI Scenarios: Boom, Mass Unemployment, Bubble Burst — Warns of Valuation Downgrade Risk - BigGo Finance
body: Is artificial intelligence (AI) the engine of a new productivity revolution, or the next capital bubble waiting to burst? Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh's answer is three economic paths that coexist simultaneously and end very differently. In opening remarks on Monday (the 16th) at a meeting of the productivity and employment task force hosted by the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco, he laid out in full for the first time three AI scenarios the Fed is internally modeling, and said plainly that the investment boom is already exerting upward pressure on inflation. Warsh noted in his prepared remarks that Fed staff have begun building models to assess how accelerated AI adoption will reshape the U.S. economy, but that these exercises are not official forecasts — they are exploratory work aimed at understanding the biggest current uncertainty. He stressed that the Fed's job is to objectively grasp AI's actual economic impact, neither to promote the technology nor to oppose it. According to Warsh's description, the first scenario is the most optimistic: AI sharply lifts productivity and economic growth, setting off a new boom in which both businesses and workers share the gains. The second is less rosy: even if economic activity expands markedly, the benefits could be offset by mass unemployment, with the fruits of technological progress not necessarily shared by workers. The third is the outcome markets least want to face: AI ultimately fails to meet expectations, and after massive capital investment and stock price gains, expected returns decline, equity valuations pull back, economic growth slows and unemployment rises more noticeably. Warsh chose his words especially carefully on the third risk path. He said the economy will eventually recover over time, but without the productivity gains originally hoped for — meaning that after the investment and stock market boom, AI's actual benefits fall short of expectations. The remarks were also read as an indirect warning about the lofty valuations of AI-related stocks. Notably, the prepared remarks used the term "Super Intelligence" (SI) throughout rather than the conventional "AI." The shift stems from an executive order signed by U.S. President Trump two months ago requiring federal departments and agencies, to the extent permitted by law, to use "Super Intelligence" in place of "artificial intelligence." Warsh described the current era as possibly the most transformative of his adult life: "SI is a new force in the economy and society, one that deserves our particular attention." On policy signals, Warsh made no comment on monetary policy or the near-term direction of interest rates, continuing his consistent style of not offering forward guidance since taking office. The entire talk focused on how AI is changing growth, productivity and the structure of employment, deliberately keeping its distance from the December rate decision. Another focus of the meeting was the formal debut of one of five external expert task forces Warsh established after becoming chair in June. The productivity and employment task force is responsible for studying AI's impact on productivity and the labor market, and its membership unusually includes tech figures, among them billionaire venture capitalist Marc Andreessen, Microsoft Executive Vice President and Xbox CEO Asha Sharma, and Stanford University scholar Charles Jones. The day's agenda also invited Stanford scholar Nick Bloom and Nikesh Arora, chairman and CEO of cybersecurity company Palo Alto Networks. Andreessen was the only task force member scheduled to attend the meeting. Under the plan, the task forces will issue recommendations around year-end, which will then be submitted to the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) for review. Bringing tech executives into the monetary policy research apparatus is unusual inside the Fed and drew outside discussion at the time. CEO Matt Murphy said, “Whatever you’ve modeled previously for custom numbers prior to the warrant definitely goes higher.” The consensus target is $310.94, with 8 Strong Buy, 35 Buy and 4 Hold ratings. Filings also noted customer concentration, China trade restrictions and $4.963 billion of long-term debt. GAAP EPS of $0.33 trailed non-GAAP. As both a benchmark and a partner through NVLink Fusion, NVIDIA ( NASDAQ:NVDA ) serves a dual role. Data Center Networking revenue rose 138%, which confirms that AI spending reaches well past GPUs and into the power, cooling, and networking suppliers we profiled in a free report on seven AI infrastructure names that aren’t chipmakers . Peers make Marvell look pricier on forward earnings. Our target sits well below consensus, so we see it as reasonable. I’m sticking with our 24/7 Wall St. price target of $232.41, a buy rated with high confidence. body: Investing.com -- Anthropic has secured its second bullish analyst initiation ahead of its highly anticipated Nasdaq debut, with New Street Research assigning a Buy rating and a $105 price target, following a similar call from KGI Securities a day earlier. New Street Research's team, including analyst Pierre Ferragu, initiated coverage on Tuesday, describing Anthropic as a "generational IPO" and arguing that artificial intelligence has a significantly larger addressable market than cloud computing. The analyst expects AI to steadily capture a growing share of knowledge-work spending over the coming decades, drawing a comparison with the expansion of cloud computing since 2010. However, he sees AI adoption spreading twice as quickly, with an addressable market 10 times larger. Ferragu's bullish investment thesis rests on three convictions: demand for AI will remain constrained by supply through 2030, both frontier and open-weight AI models have sustainable business models and substantial market opportunities, and Anthropic is currently best positioned among frontier AI developers. He also argued that the upcoming IPO offers investors an attractive valuation multiple. The initiation follows KGI Securities' decision on Monday to begin coverage with an Outperform rating and a $100 price target, giving Anthropic two positive analyst ratings before its shares begin trading. Both targets imply substantial upside relative to the company's expected IPO price range of $70 to $78. Based on the $74 midpoint, KGI's target implies approximately 35% upside, while New Street's $105 target represents approximately 42%. Stop chasing stocks after they've already rallied. Join today! » The early endorsements are particularly noteworthy because much of Wall Street is participating in Anthropic's IPO and cannot immediately publish conventional research coverage. Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley are leading the offering, alongside JPMorgan, Citigroup, Deutsche Bank, UBS, BNP Paribas and Crédit Agricole, among others. Investment banks participating in an IPO face restrictions designed to prevent analysts from promoting a company while their firms are seeking underwriting business or distributing its shares. FINRA rules also impose a minimum 10-day post-IPO quiet period on firms participating as underwriters or dealers. In practice, underwriting syndicates commonly observe a longer research blackout, often around 25 days. The restrictions are intended to protect research independence and prevent investment banks from using favorable analyst recommendations to support an offering. As a result, independent firms outside the underwriting syndicate can establish their views and publish price targets before many of the largest Wall Street research departments enter the picture. That gives KGI Securities and New Street Research an opportunity to shape the initial investment narrative around Anthropic before the major underwriting banks begin issuing their own coverage. Anthropic still expects to price its IPO between $70 and $78 per share. title: Microsoft Stock Has Grown Roughly 14-Fold Since Satya Nadella Became CEO in 2014, a 23% Annual Growth Rate. Can That Pace Continue Under Heavy AI Spending? - Yahoo Finance
body: Satya Nadella took the reins as CEO of Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) in 2014, following Steve Ballmer's 14-year tenure. Ballmer managed to take Microsoft's revenue from $23 billion in the year he took over to $87 billion by the time he left. Net income climbed 135% in those 14 years. But the stock price ended up in practically the same place it was when he took over, due in part to the government's antitrust suit against Microsoft, the dot-com bubble popping, and the Great Recession in 2008. Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » During his tenure, Nadella has focused heavily on the potential of its cloud computing business, which includes Azure and Microsoft 365. Both have produced fantastic results for Microsoft, and its Windows operating system is taking a back seat to those growing businesses these days. Overall, the stock is up more than 14-fold since Nadella took over as CEO, a 23% annualized pace. But with Microsoft spending huge sums every year to grow its data center infrastructure amid the AI boom, investors are wondering whether it can maintain that torrid pace. Microsoft's AI spending has grown considerably over the last few years. Management expects to spend $170 billion on capital expenditures this year, including $50 billion in the final three months of 2026. CFO Amy Hood says that the budget for 2027 will be even bigger. Those capital expenditures are huge bets, and making them has required Microsoft to raise outside capital. It recently sold $25 billion worth of debt at interest rates ranging from 4.85% to 6.35%. The question investors need to ask is whether Microsoft can produce returns on its invested capital above that cost of capital. Management has assured investors the answer is a resounding yes. "We feel good [about] the return on every dollar of capex we're spending. We're confident in that," CFO Amy Hood said on the company's first-quarter earnings call, answering a question about raising capital. "As we continue to improve the efficiencies of our infrastructure, each dollar of capex has the potential to support more revenue and higher returns over time." However, not all of Microsoft's AI spending will show up as Azure revenue growth. Hood noted that many resources go toward Microsoft's own products and development, which holds back potential Azure revenue growth. That shows up in its Microsoft 365 sales growth, particularly the growing adoption of Copilot. In its most recent quarterly update, Microsoft said it had 30 million paid Copilot users, but it counts over 450 million Microsoft 365 users. Both Azure and Microsoft 365 are growing quickly, and that trend is expected to continue for the foreseeable future as capex increases. Azure sales climbed 48% year over year last quarter, accelerating from 43% the quarter before. Microsoft 365 sales increased 17%, accelerating for its commercial segment. Realistically, 23% annualized share price growth is a high bar to meet. Theoretically, the stock should only increase as quickly as management improves earnings per share. In practice, however, that's rarely the case. Investors are willing to pay more or less for each dollar of earnings depending on how optimistic they are about the future. With the strong growth of Microsoft's cloud computing business and the potential for free cash flow to rise in the years following the big step-up in investment, Microsoft could retire a lot of shares while growing its overall earnings. That should result in very strong earnings-per-share growth, but 23% may be asking a lot over the medium- to long-run. With Huang gone, investors are looking for clues about Nvidia’s future, from billions of dollars invested in cloud providers, suppliers and AI startups to who will ultimately lead the world’s most valuable chipmaker. The AI boom’s most prolific salesman resigned on Thursday after revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang and two Nvidia employees. U.S. intelligence agencies are trying to determine the extent of her ties to China’s Ministry of State Security and what information she may have passed to Beijing, according to two people familiar with the matter. Huang’s exit ended three decades of founder-led control over Nvidia’s chip roadmap, customer deals and Washington ties, making execution a bigger risk than near-term AI demand, analysts say. Finance chief Colette Kress is interim CEO, while the board considers internal and external candidates. A growing “Stand With Jensen” campaign has complicated the search, although the board is not considering Huang’s return, three people told Reuters on Monday. Huang said on Tuesday he would be “honored” to return if the board deemed it best. Earlier on Tuesday, Nvidia’s board created a committee on national security and export controls, its first major governance move since Huang’s departure, as scrutiny grows over the chipmaker’s national security role. Washington has also tightened licensing rules for chip shipments to Southeast Asia and overseas data centres serving Chinese firms, while lawmakers prepare to question Huang, who had pushed for greater chip exports to China. Investors were already uneasy about AI spending after Democrats’ midterm sweep fueled fears of tougher scrutiny and slower data-centre expansion. They also want to know whether Nvidia’s next CEO will continue financing customers, a practice critics call circular. Tuesday’s results offer a first read on Vera Rubin, Nvidia’s newest generation of AI processors and successor to Grace Blackwell. Nvidia said in August that Vera Rubin would account for about a fifth of data centre revenue in the October quarter and forecast 70 per cent revenue growth in the next fiscal year. Reporting by Anhata Rooprai in Bengaluru; Editing by Shinjini Ganguli and Anil D’Silva

body: In its first report since Jensen Huang resigned, Nvidia beat Wall Street's forecasts on revenue, profit and guidance. Revenue more than doubled to $115.8 billion, the company forecast $130 billion for the current quarter and raised its growth target for next year to 75%. Adjusted earnings per share were $2.68, against expectations of about $2.47. • Data Center revenue reached $107.6 billion, up 110%, and Nvidia said its next-generation Vera Rubin NVL72 platform has started shipping. • Guidance: fourth-quarter revenue of $130 billion, plus or minus 3%, above the consensus of about $125 billion. Revenue from AI cloud providers, industrial customers and enterprises grew 195% to $47.5 billion, although that came in slightly below the $48.4 billion analysts had expected. Nvidia also said Vera Rubin NVL72, the successor to its Blackwell systems, has shipped. In August, Kress had said Rubin would make up about a fifth of third-quarter Data Center revenue, so a smooth ramp was one of the key tests for this report. This was Kress's first earnings call as interim CEO, after Huang's resignation on 12 November. Her central message was continuity. Asked about the state of the company, she said it is 'business as usual at Nvidia'. Investors had worried that Nvidia might withdraw its forecast of 70% growth for the fiscal year ending in January 2028. Instead, Kress raised it, telling investors Nvidia now expects revenue to rise 75%. That was arguably the most important number of the night, because it suggests customers are not pausing orders because of the leadership crisis. Earlier on Tuesday, Huang had said he would be open to returning as CEO if the board thought that was in shareholders' best interest. title: Nvidia stock rises after hours as revenue forecast beats estimates - TradingView
body: Nvidia shares NVDA rose 2.47% in after-hours trading on Tuesday after the chipmaker delivered a stronger-than-expected revenue forecast for its January quarter, signalling that demand for artificial intelligence hardware remains robust despite leadership uncertainty and concerns about industry spending. The company forecast revenue of $130 billion for its fiscal fourth quarter, plus or minus 3%, compared with the $125.3 billion expected by analysts tracked by FactSet. The outlook does not include any data-centre revenue from China. The forecast followed another record quarter for Nvidia, with revenue and earnings both exceeding Wall Street expectations. Investors had been closely watching the results amid the departure of longtime CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned last week following reports about his personal relationships. Nvidia expects revenue of approximately $130 billion in the quarter ending in January. The forecast exceeded analyst expectations and suggests that demand for the company's AI chips and computing systems remains strong. The company also expects a gross margin of around 71.5% in the quarter. The outlook was particularly important given speculation about whether Nvidia would provide a quarterly forecast amid the uncertainty surrounding its leadership. Nvidia's third-quarter revenue increased 103% year-over-year to $115.8 billion, surpassing the approximately $109 billion expected by analysts. Net income reached $65.3 billion, while earnings per share came in at $2.68, above the FactSet consensus estimate of $2.48. Demand for Nvidia's AI hardware remained strong during the quarter as the company began shipments of its latest Vera Rubin systems. The results provide further evidence of continued investment in AI infrastructure, although concerns remain about whether spending across the industry can maintain its current pace. Nvidia returned $28.1 billion to shareholders during the quarter ended October 25 through share repurchases and dividends. The figure exceeded the previous quarterly record of $26 billion, set in the preceding quarter. Share buybacks accounted for $22.1 billion of the latest shareholder returns. Nvidia has now spent $62 billion on repurchases during the first three quarters of its fiscal year, significantly more than the $40.4 billion spent during the previous fiscal year. The company still has $227.3 billion available under its existing share repurchase programme. The scale of the buybacks highlights Nvidia's ability to return substantial capital to shareholders while continuing to invest in its AI hardware business. Nvidia's strong results came during a period of significant leadership uncertainty. Huang resigned last Thursday following reports of multiple extramarital relationships, including one involving a company employee and another involving a woman suspected by US officials of having links to Chinese intelligence. Former CFO Colette Kress is serving as interim CEO while Nvidia looks for a permanent replacement. The company has also elevated board member Harvey Jones to chairman, marking the first time Nvidia has had someone in that role. Earlier on Tuesday, Huang said he would be willing to return if the board decided that his reinstatement would be in the company's best interests. However, a person familiar with the board's thinking told Wall Street Journal that it was not considering bringing him back. Nvidia's board has also formed a committee to oversee national security policies and compliance with US export controls. Huang and General Counsel Tim Teter have agreed to brief three House committees in early December as lawmakers seek answers about the company's exports to Asia. Nvidia's revenue rose to $115.8 billion, compared with $57 billion a year ago. Wall Street analysts had expected third-quarter revenue of nearly $109 billion, according to financial research firm FactSet. The financial results represent the first time Nvidia has reported earnings without Huang at the helm of the chip company he cofounded in 1993. The chip firm reported third-quarter data center revenue of $107.6 billion, up 110% from one year ago, marking a record. "Our momentum is real. Nvidia is an exceptional technology leader, powered by the relentless innovation of our people," Kress, who also serves as Nvidia's chief financial officer, said in a statement. During the earnings call, Kress and new Nvidia board chair Harvey Jones declined to answer questions about the company's progress in finding a permanent chief executive. But Jones said that the company "does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO." The company's search for a new chief is underway, Jones added, noting the company is considering both internal and external candidates to replace Huang. In the meantime, the board has "every confidence" in Kress' ability to lead the company, Jones said. Nvidia shares rose nearly 4%, to $161.57, in after-hours trading. Adam Crisafulli, a Wall Street analyst with Vital Knowledge, said Nvidia's stronger-than-expected results should boost investor confidence. "The headline numbers for [the fiscal third quarter] are strong, and the FQ4 guide is solid, too. Given how depressed sentiment is, this should be enough to spur a rebound," he said in a note to investors. Huang resigned last week after admitting he had an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence has identified as a Chinese spy. Beyond spurring his shock exit from the company, the scandal has raised questions over whether the company's advanced chips were being used in China in violation of export controls. The U.S. government is moving to close any loopholes in those rules. The Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security on Monday issued an interim rule limiting other countries' access to advanced chips that power artificial intelligence. Kress addressed the new export controls in Tuesday's call, saying that "with demand far exceeding supply, we expect our performance to remain strong." The company will study the new export controls, she added. On Tuesday, Nvidia's board also said it formed a new committee to ensure that the company's policies comply with U.S. export controls.
